observations.author: self
observations.text:
Leaders love the word "progress." And yet only a few can actually point to what changed.

Attending a workshop isn't progress. 
Feeling inspired for a week isn't progress. 

Progress is a specific behaviour, done differently, that you can point to a month later.

This is where most leadership development fails: insight without a mechanism to turn it into a new default behaviour.

Theoretical learning is important. Putting it into practice once is even better. What will make a lasting change is continuous repetition. That will build a new habit, and hence that will be real progress. 

What's one thing you did differently this month that you can actually point to?
And if there's nothing - what is the first thing you want to change? 

#Leadership #MAP #Progress

observations.author: self
observations.text:
Blindspots can cost you your career. 

That is not because you're incompetent. It is because you're the last person to see the pattern everyone else already sees.

The colleague who thinks they're "direct" but reads as dismissive in every meeting. The manager who believes they're empowering their team but is actually avoiding hard conversations. The leader convinced they thrive under pressure while their team quietly burns out around them.

Nobody chooses these patterns on purpose. That's what makes a blindspot a blindspot: it is invisible from the inside. In a career, invisible patterns don't stay invisible. They show up as the promotion you didn't get, the feedback that keeps repeating, the team that keeps turning over. By the time it's obvious to you, it's been obvious to everyone else for years.

This is where the Hogan assessment earns its reputation. It doesn't just measure how you see yourself. It gives you three lenses: how you come across at your best (bright side), how you derail under pressure (dark side), and what actually drives you (values and motives).

That dark side data is the one most people never get honestly. Those traits hide behind your strengths until pressure exposes them and by then, they're already shaping how people see you.

What changes when you see it clearly: you stop mistaking self-awareness for actual awareness, get language for patterns you'd only felt vaguely uneasy about, and get the chance to manage a trait before it manages you: in the meeting, the 1:1, the moment that decides whether you get the room or lose it.

Careers rarely stall from a lack of talent. They stall because a blindspot quietly outpaces it. Hogan won't fix that for you, but it hands you the mirror most people never get.

Want to see your own blindspots before they cost you? Send me a DM or comment "hogan" and I'll set you up with a Hogan assessment.

observations.author: self
observations.text:
It was a pleasure and great opportunity to be a guest with the esteemed host Ms. Cyba Audi on the morning show “Al Sabah with Cyba” (The Morning with Cyba)  from Dubai.  We introduced the topic of Emotional intelligence (EI).  A skill that was once soft but is slowly proving to be a necessity and a gage of growth and success.  EI is gaining momentum and quickly becoming a competitive advantage to companies and leaders that implement EI as a criteria for hiring and developing employees and leaders alike.  In fact EI is starting to impact, growth, market share, productivity, employee engagement and many crucial success factors to any organization.
Defining Emotional intelligence is always a good starting point to insure alignment on the topic discussed. EI, simply speaking, is the process of understanding and regulating emotions to assist in improving the quality of the thought process in oneself while understanding the emotions of others to assist in cultivating better relationships with others.
EI is divided into two parts and each part is divided into two components.  The first part is related to the self and that is divided into self-awareness and emotional regulation.  The second part is related to the others and it is divided into social awareness and cultivating relationships.  Empathy falls under the social aspect of EI.
The first component of EI is self-awareness and a key point that was highlighted was the fact that any decision we make passes through an emotional filter first.  Hence, it is imperative that this filter is accurate to improve the quality and accuracy of our decisions. To achieve that one must understand themselves and understand their triggers and their emotions.
We further highlighted that it is important for professionals and and even more so leaders to regulate their emotions instead of controlling them. Controlling emotions in a suppressive manner prevents the person from processing what they are feeling and acting accordingly.  In general, emotions serve as a feedback process; they help extract the data and the information that the emotion is communicating for the sake of understanding how to behave and what decisions to make or actions to take.
One important consideration is that leaders and people of power have the ability to pass on emotions to their team members and this process is called “Emotion contagion.”  Therefore, accuracy of emotions and regulation are crucial to the well-being of any relationship and organization.
Finally and perhaps the most important take away about emotional intelligence is that Emotional intelligence is a skill that can be adopted, developed and cultivated in any individual that is interested in improving their relationship with themselves and others.  In addition a high emotional quotient can contribute directly in a more successful career and a closer connection with others.

observations.author: self
observations.text:
Individual performance is a leadership illusion.
We have become incredibly good at measuring what individuals achieve.

Who exceeded their targets?
Who delivered the project?
Who needs coaching?
Who deserves the promotion?

It's neat. It's measurable. It gives us the comforting impression that performance belongs to individuals.
I don't believe it does. I believe that while individuals need performance guidance, this is only part of the picture.

I have worked with exceptionally talented people who looked like average performers because they were part of a dysfunctional team. I've also seen fairly ordinary individuals achieve extraordinary results because they were part of a team that trusted one another, challenged one another, and worked towards a common purpose.

The difference wasn't the individual.
It was the system they were operating in.

When a team is struggling, we instinctively ask, "Who's underperforming?" We look for the weak link, the difficult employee, or the person who needs fixing. That question assumes performance lives inside people. It only partly does.

What if there was more thought to the performance of the individuals in the team?
What if performance is created, supported, or constrained by the relationships and team dynamics around them?

What if, instead of asking who needs to change, we began asking what's happening within the team that's producing those results? If instead of fixing individuals, we became curious about the patterns, dynamics, and relationships influencing everyone's performance.

How different would your leadership conversations be if you stopped measuring people in isolation and started looking at the system they are part of?

Mireia Mujika: Hi everyone and welcome to this new episode of “Ways to Grow” podcast... My name is Mireia Mujika. I’m a personal and executive coach. And for this episode, I have invited Linda Berlot to join us. Linda is an entrepreneur and a certified executive and team coach. She is a PCC or professional certified coach and an ORSC organization and relationship system coach certified by the ICF, the international coaching federation. She is the founder and CEO of Berlot group, which is a team coaching organization and she's a partner for CRR global... Linda is Italian and has been living in the UAE and working in the region since 2004. Her clients include Emirates, EMBD, Mar, Electrolux, SCB, Cleveland clinic, Michelin and many others across all industries.
Linda Berlot: Well, ORSC stands for organization and relationship systems coaching. It's a model of coaching systems. A system is either a pair or a team, a family, a group and actually as an individual inside us is the first system. So, it's a model of coaching which helps us coach the system as one united entity rather than coaching the individuals in the team or the system.
Linda Berlot: You know, I think, as coaches we are all different, right? Some people are really thrilled about coaching the individual and they love that. I feel lost doing that. I find myself coaching a large group or a system... What I love about systems coaching is the magic it creates. And I don't use that word lightly. For me, when we learn how to be in better relationship with each other, with ourselves first and then with each other. Or in teams, if we support them to be, for their team dynamics, to be more skillful and healthier, they start to be more productive. And I love to see that.
Linda Berlot: I love that question. I can't tell you how many of my CEOs or team leaders have said to me, Linda, can you please coach my team? Because that person, and if that person doesn't change, they or other people are going to have to leave. And the first thing that we do is we educate the team leader and the team themselves that all behavior belongs to the team because it's in the dynamic that we are toxic.
